PHẦN A: 1. In many low-income regions, rice and other cheap grains still provide basic sustenance for families who cannot afford a more varied diet. — "Sustenance" là danh từ không đếm được, trang trọng hơn "food"; hay đi với "provide/basic sustenance", nhấn mạnh vai trò duy trì sự sống chứ không phải thưởng thức. 2. Studying the regional dishes of southern Italy convinced me that gastronomy can reveal as much about a culture's history as its literature or art. — "Gastronomy" chỉ nghệ thuật/thực hành ẩm thực nói chung, khác với "gastroenterology" (chuyên khoa tiêu hoá); thường dùng trong văn phong học thuật hoặc trang trọng. 3. Because leafy greens and soft fruit are highly perishable, supermarkets are increasingly organising their supply chains around faster delivery and better cold storage. — "Perishable" là tính từ mô tả thực phẩm dễ hỏng; collocation phổ biến "highly perishable", "perishable goods/items". 4. To combat hidden micronutrient deficiencies, many countries now require that basic flour sold in shops be fortified with iron and folic acid. — "Fortified" luôn đi với giới từ "with" (fortified with + chất dinh dưỡng), chỉ việc bổ sung vitamin/khoáng chất vào thực phẩm. 5. Rice remains the dietary staple for more than half of the world's population, even as diets diversify in wealthier cities. — "Staple" (danh từ) nghĩa là thực phẩm chính; khi làm tính từ đứng trước danh từ ("staple diet/food") không thêm "-s". 6. Consumers who choose imported avocados and berries over local produce are, often without realising it, dramatically increasing their food miles. — "Food miles" luôn ở số nhiều, chỉ quãng đường thực phẩm di chuyển từ nơi sản xuất đến người tiêu dùng — thước đo tác động môi trường. 7. Ancient moralists tended to view overeating as a sign of gluttony rather than as a predictable response to food engineered to be irresistible. — "Gluttony" là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ sự ăn uống vô độ; tính từ tương ứng là "gluttonous", danh từ chỉ người là "glutton". 8. Nutritionists argue that many packaged snacks are specifically designed to delay the feeling of satiety, encouraging people to keep eating long after they are full. — "Satiety" là cảm giác no/thoả mãn sau khi ăn; hay đi với "a feeling of satiety", "reach satiety"; đối lập với "hunger/appetite". 9. Chronic malnutrition is not limited to poorer countries; it can also affect people in wealthier nations who eat plenty of calories but few genuine nutrients. — "Malnutrition" bao gồm cả thiếu và thừa dinh dưỡng mất cân bằng, không chỉ nghĩa "thiếu ăn"; collocation "chronic malnutrition", "suffer from malnutrition". 10. Reading the label on a packet of crisps, I was startled by how many artificial additives were needed simply to keep the flavour consistent. — "Additives" (số nhiều) là các chất được thêm vào thực phẩm để cải thiện hương vị, hình thức hoặc hạn sử dụng; collocation "artificial/food additives". 11. Public health researchers increasingly agree that diets high in salt, sugar and refined carbohydrates can be seriously detrimental to long-term health. — "Detrimental" luôn đi với giới từ "to" (detrimental to health), nghĩa là có hại, gây tổn hại dần dần. 12. Travelling through Vietnam, I was struck by how much regional cuisine varies from north to south, shaped by climate, history and available ingredients. — "Cuisine" là danh từ không đếm được chỉ phong cách/nền ẩm thực đặc trưng của một vùng hay quốc gia; collocation "local/indigenous/fusion cuisine".

Band 8: Given its typically high fat and sugar content, it is hardly surprising that fast food is regarded by many nutritionists as detrimental to public health. 2. Band 7: Many people have stopped cooking at home simply because their busy work schedules leave them with very little time to spare. Band 8: So demanding have modern working schedules become that home cooking has, for many time-poor households, been all but replaced by convenience food. 3. Band 7: I would tentatively suggest that people should prioritise locally grown food over imported produce wherever possible. Band 8: Were consumers to prioritise locally sourced produce over imported alternatives, the resulting reduction in food miles would likely bring meaningful environmental benefits. 4. Band 7: Some children consume excessive amounts of sugar partly because advertising tends to present sweet products as fun and desirable. Band 8: It is largely the persuasive architecture of advertising, rather than taste alone, that appears to drive excessive sugar consumption among children. 5. Band 7: Traditional cooking methods seem to be gradually disappearing as younger generations increasingly opt for convenient, ready-made meals. Band 8: What is often mistaken for a simple shift in taste is, in reality, the gradual erosion of traditional culinary heritage under the pressure of convenience culture. 6. Band 7: Governments should arguably introduce stricter regulations to prevent companies from marketing unhealthy food directly to children. Band 8: There is growing concern that, absent stricter regulation, companies will continue to target children with the marketing of nutritionally poor products. 7. Band 7: Emerging agricultural technology could potentially help farmers produce food in ways that place less strain on the environment. Band 8: While technology may well ease the environmental burden of food production, it would be unwise to treat it as a sufficient solution in itself. 8. Band 7: Dining out on a regular basis can prove costly and does not necessarily guarantee a balanced, healthy diet. Band 8: Frequent dining out, for all its convenience, often comes at a considerable financial cost without necessarily delivering nutritional benefit.

passages.text: For the better part of half a century, dietary guidelines in industrialised countries have rested on a comparatively confident set of claims. Saturated fat, the official advice ran, should be limited; refined carbohydrate was tolerated; salt was to be cut; and fruit, vegetables and whole grains were to be eaten in abundance. Successive editions of the United States Dietary Guidelines, first issued in 1980, have repeated versions of these recommendations with only modest revisions. Yet the empirical foundations on which they rest have become the subject of a sustained and at times bitter argument, one that has spilled from specialist journals into the pages of broadsheet newspapers. The dispute matters because nutrition advice, more than almost any other branch of public health, reaches every household.
passages.title: What Should We Eat?

passages.text: The most influential defender of the conventional approach is Professor Walter Willett of Harvard's School of Public Health, whose Nurses' Health Study has tracked the dietary patterns of more than two hundred thousand participants since the late 1970s. Willett maintains that long-running observational cohorts, despite their well-known limitations, have repeatedly identified the same set of beneficial foods — vegetables, whole grains, nuts and oily fish — and the same set of cautionary ones, including processed meat and sugar-sweetened drinks. The convergence of findings across countries and decades, he argues, is unlikely to be coincidental. While conceding that no single observational study can establish causation, he contends that the cumulative weight of evidence is sufficient to justify the broad direction of present guidelines, even where individual associations remain modest.
passages.title: What Should We Eat?

passages.text: A vigorous challenge has come from the methodologist Professor John Ioannidis of Stanford University, whose 2018 commentary in the Journal of the American Medical Association proved especially provocative. Ioannidis points out that nutritional epidemiology relies overwhelmingly on dietary questionnaires whose accuracy is, in his view, dubious. Participants are asked to recall what they ate over months or years, and small reporting errors are magnified when the data are combined. Worse, when the same dataset is interrogated with thousands of plausible analytic choices, researchers may report only those associations that reach statistical significance, leaving the rest unpublished. The result, Ioannidis argues, is a literature in which almost every food appears, at some point, to be linked with almost every disease. Such findings, he suggests, should be treated with considerable scepticism, and dietary guidelines anchored on them rest on shakier ground than their authors typically acknowledge.
passages.title: What Should We Eat?

passages.text: Between these two poles, a third position has gained traction. Professor Dariush Mozaffarian, formerly of Tufts University, accepts that observational nutrition research has genuine limitations but rejects the proposal to discount it wholesale. The right response, he argues, is methodological reform rather than retreat: better dietary assessment using digital diaries and biomarkers, pre-registered analytic plans, and clearer separation between hypothesis-generating studies and confirmatory ones. He also urges a shift in framing. Rather than debating whether individual nutrients are good or bad, researchers and regulators should classify foods by their degree of industrial processing, an approach already adopted in Brazilian guidelines and increasingly under consideration elsewhere. The evidence linking heavily processed foods to weight gain and cardiometabolic disease, Mozaffarian contends, is now substantial and difficult to dismiss on methodological grounds alone.
passages.title: What Should We Eat?

passages.text: The author finds Mozaffarian's middle path the most defensible. Ioannidis's critique, while bracingly honest about the field's weaknesses, risks paralysing public health authorities who must give some advice while imperfect evidence is improved. The blanket dismissal of observational nutrition would leave a vacuum that commercial interests would quickly fill, often with less rigour and more confidence than the academy can muster. At the same time, Willett's defence of the existing framework, although understandable from a researcher with five decades of investment in cohort studies, sometimes underplays the genuine confusion produced by contradictory headline findings that he himself acknowledges in private correspondence. The general public, faced with weekly reports announcing that coffee, eggs or red meat have been newly vindicated or condemned, may reasonably conclude that the experts cannot agree on anything.
passages.title: What Should We Eat?

passages.text: A separate and perhaps deeper question is whether dietary guidelines should be technical documents at all. The sociologist Professor Marion Nestle of New York University has argued for many years that the production of national nutrition advice is shaped by political and commercial pressures as much as by science. Industry lobbying, she notes, has at various times softened guideline language on sugar, processed meat and saturated dairy fat. Nestle's analysis, which the author regards as more difficult to refute than its detractors generally admit, implies that even a methodologically transformed nutritional science would not, on its own, deliver guidelines that the public could fully trust. The institutions issuing the advice must themselves be insulated from interests whose primary concern is the volume of food sold rather than the population's long-term health.
passages.title: What Should We Eat?

passages.text: On balance, the field appears to be moving in three directions at once. Better measurement tools are entering use; the focus is broadening from individual nutrients to whole dietary patterns and degrees of processing; and a small but growing literature, including several large randomised trials of Mediterranean-style diets, is providing the kind of causal evidence that has long been missing. Whether these changes will be sufficient to restore public confidence is less certain. The author suspects they will not, unless they are accompanied by greater transparency about funding, conflicts of interest and the genuine uncertainty that pervades parts of the discipline. Honest acknowledgement of what is not yet known may, perhaps counter-intuitively, prove a stronger foundation for trustworthy dietary guidance than premature confidence has ever been.

audio_scripts.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture wraps our nutritional epidemiology block — focusing specifically on dietary diversity and gut-microbiome resilience in middle-aged adults. [pause:5s] The conceptual framework I'll be drawing on this morning is taken from the work of Professor Joaquin Bezuidenhout — that's B-E-Z-U-I-D-E-N-H-O-U-T, no hyphen, no apostrophe, the H is pronounced. Bezuidenhout's 2017 monograph reframed dietary-pattern research from a single-nutrient deficit model into what he calls "phytochemical breadth theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The longitudinal nutrition cohort I'll reference today was first recruited in 2008 — sorry, let me correct that, 2007; the published descriptive statistics in 2008 covered baseline food-frequency data collected throughout 2007. So whenever I refer to the Bezuidenhout baseline year, please record 2007. [pause:3s] Right. A quick tense-orientation note, because the assessment methodology has changed materially across two decades. Dietary intake USED TO be captured almost exclusively with seven-day weighed food diaries; NOW the field deploys mixed methods combining diaries with stool-based 16S rRNA sequencing and smartphone meal-imaging algorithms; and from 2029 a pan-European consortium WILL be rolling out continuous glucose monitors as the primary metabolic readout. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT mixed-methods state — that is, diaries plus stool sequencing. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The dietary phenomenon Bezuidenhout foregrounds — the cumulative number of distinct plant species an individual consumes weekly — is termed "phytochemical breadth". Now, you'll meet related labels in the older literature: plant variety, dietary heterogeneity, vegetable richness. These all gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Bezuidenhout's construct. The currently accepted scholarly term is phytochemical breadth — p-h-y-t-o-chemical breadth. So when the older literature uses plant variety or dietary heterogeneity, those are related but distinct constructs. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to address is what nutritionists call the "microbiome resilience continuum". When clinicians describe how an individual's gut flora recovers from an antibiotic course, they sketch a graded continuum running from rapid recolonisation through delayed partial recovery to persistent dysbiosis. So, you know, you'LL see a patient who bounces back to baseline diversity within two weeks — that's rapid recolonisation. Or a patient whose flora still looks depleted six months later — that's persistent dysbiosis. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the microbiome resilience continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the cohort data — and pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the five hundred and forty participants we tracked across three city sites last spring, MOST reported consuming fewer than fifteen distinct plant species in a typical week — roughly sixty-two per cent. Only a few — about eight per cent — exceeded the thirty-species threshold associated with maximal microbiome diversity, and some — thirty per cent — fell into an intermediate range. So low breadth dominates numerically, but the high-breadth tail, though small, is clinically important. [pause:3s] A second construct I want to flag is "dietary monotony". This refers to a temporal pattern in which an individual's weekly intake repeats the same fifteen or so ingredients with minimal rotation. At our Westfield clinic site, our team logged one hundred and twelve documented monotony episodes across the cohort during one twelve-week observation window. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that simply increasing daily fibre intake automatically broadens microbial diversity is, frankly, not supported. Most of the participants in our sample did NOT show the predicted monotonic gain in alpha-diversity scores as raw fibre grams increased. Quite the opposite — many displayed a plateau response, with no further diversity gains above twenty-five grams a day. So the older "fibre-dose hypothesis", which predicts linear gains, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in the afternoon seminar. I want you to focus on the stool-sequencing protocols specifically, not the future glucose-monitor deployment or the legacy diary-only instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: dietary patterns are best modelled as phytochemical breadth, not single-nutrient deficits; the technical term for plant-species count is phytochemical breadth; low-breadth eating dominates the cohort at roughly sixty-two per cent; and the fibre-dose hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'LL examine fermented-food interventions. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

Overall, the process is essentially linear and one-directional, and it can be divided into three broad phases: agricultural production at origin, industrial processing, and final refinement in the consumer country. The early, farm-based stages are notably more labour-intensive than the mechanised stages that follow.

Initially, coffee shrubs are cultivated on highland farms, after which the ripe red cherries are harvested either by hand or by machine. The cherries are then pulped to remove the outer skin and subsequently fermented in water tanks for up to 48 hours in order to dissolve the mucilage. Once fermentation is complete, the beans are sun-dried on patios or in mechanical dryers until their moisture content falls to roughly 11%.

In the next phase, the parchment layer is hulled off and the green beans are graded by size and density before being exported abroad in jute sacks. Finally, in the destination country, the beans are roasted at high temperatures, then ground, packaged and brewed, generating considerable food miles before the coffee reaches the consumer's cup.

blocks.text: The sharp rise of ultra-processed food on supermarket shelves has, in recent decades, become a serious public-health concern. This essay will examine the principal drivers behind this trend before suggesting a set of practical measures.

The causes of the crisis appear to be largely structural rather than purely personal. What food companies exploit, above all, is the aggressive marketing of cheap, energy-dense products engineered for hyper-palatability. Such snacks routinely bypass the body's natural feeling of satiety, encouraging overconsumption. In addition, dual-income households often lack the time to prepare meals from scratch, which makes processed alternatives the default option. The result is a rapid rise in obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, particularly in low-income communities where fresh produce is least affordable and where these cheap staples are most heavily promoted.

In terms of remedies, governments must intervene on several fronts. A sugar levy, similar to those introduced in the UK and Mexico, is believed to have pushed beverage companies to reformulate their recipes and trim sugar content nationwide. Clear front-of-pack labelling, together with restrictions on advertising to children, is likely to curb impulse consumption among the most vulnerable shoppers. Beyond such fiscal tools, schools should embed nutritional literacy in the curriculum so that pupils learn to interpret labels and assess food miles.

It is also important that fresh produce be made more affordable through targeted subsidies, otherwise lower-income families will continue to depend on cheaper processed staples. To conclude, the ultra-processed food crisis is driven not so much by individual weakness as by a commercially engineered environment, so a coordinated mix of fiscal, educational and regulatory measures is essential.

The proliferation of ultra-processed food has emerged as one of the defining public-health challenges of our era, implicated in surging rates of obesity, metabolic disease and premature mortality. The causes are largely commercial-structural, and any credible response must combine fiscal, educational and regulatory levers.

The crisis is driven not so much by individual gluttony as by a tightly engineered food environment. Industry data indicate that ultra-processed products now supply a substantial share of dietary energy in many high-income countries, while penetration in middle-income markets is accelerating. So aggressively are these foods reformulated for hyper-palatability that they routinely override innate satiety signals, fostering overconsumption. Compounding this, time-poor dual-income households turn to convenience formats, and the commodification of food has rendered ultra-processed snacks both cheaper and more accessible than fresh, perishable produce — especially in lower-income neighbourhoods.

A coherent policy response is therefore imperative. Sugar and fat levies, such as those operating in the UK and Mexico, are believed to have driven measurable reformulation and modest reductions in consumption. Equally crucial is mandatory front-of-pack labelling, coupled with restrictions on advertising high-fat, salt and sugar products to children, a measure the World Health Organisation has long advocated. What schools must also undertake is the cultivation of genuine nutritional literacy, equipping pupils to interpret labelling, food miles and ingredient lists rather than absorb marketing claims uncritically.

Only if fresh produce is rendered economically competitive — through targeted subsidies and support for short supply chains — will lower-income households realistically shift away from ultra-processed staples. 1. In many low-income regions, rice and other cheap grains still provide basic (SUSTENANCE) for families who cannot afford a more varied diet.
2. Studying the regional dishes of southern Italy convinced me that (GASTRONOMY) can reveal as much about a culture's history as its literature or art.
3. Because leafy greens and soft fruit are highly (PERISHABLE), supermarkets are increasingly organising their supply chains around faster delivery and better cold storage.
4. To combat hidden micronutrient deficiencies, many countries now require that basic flour sold in shops be (FORTIFIED) with iron and folic acid.
5. Rice remains the dietary (STAPLE) for more than half of the world's population, even as diets diversify in wealthier cities.

7. Ancient moralists tended to view overeating as a sign of (GLUTTONY) rather than as a predictable response to food engineered to be irresistible.
8. Nutritionists argue that many packaged snacks are specifically designed to delay the feeling of (SATIETY), encouraging people to keep eating long after they are full.
9. Chronic (MALNUTRITION) is not limited to poorer countries; it can also affect people in wealthier nations who eat plenty of calories but few genuine nutrients.
10. Reading the label on a packet of crisps, I was startled by how many artificial (ADDITIVES) were needed simply to keep the flavour consistent.

PHẦN A: 1. In many low-income regions, rice and other cheap grains still provide basic sustenance for families who cannot afford a more varied diet. — "Sustenance" là danh từ không đếm được, trang trọng hơn "food"; hay đi với "provide/basic sustenance", nhấn mạnh vai trò duy trì sự sống chứ không phải thưởng thức. 2. Studying the regional dishes of southern Italy convinced me that gastronomy can reveal as much about a culture's history as its literature or art. — "Gastronomy" chỉ nghệ thuật/thực hành ẩm thực nói chung, khác với "gastroenterology" (chuyên khoa tiêu hoá); thường dùng trong văn phong học thuật hoặc trang trọng. 3. Because leafy greens and soft fruit are highly perishable, supermarkets are increasingly organising their supply chains around faster delivery and better cold storage. — "Perishable" là tính từ mô tả thực phẩm dễ hỏng; collocation phổ biến "highly perishable", "perishable goods/items". 4. To combat hidden micronutrient deficiencies, many countries now require that basic flour sold in shops be fortified with iron and folic acid. — "Fortified" luôn đi với giới từ "with" (fortified with + chất dinh dưỡng), chỉ việc bổ sung vitamin/khoáng chất vào thực phẩm. 5. Rice remains the dietary staple for more than half of the world's population, even as diets diversify in wealthier cities. — "Staple" (danh từ) nghĩa là thực phẩm chính; khi làm tính từ đứng trước danh từ ("staple diet/food") không thêm "-s". 6. Consumers who choose imported avocados and berries over local produce are, often without realising it, dramatically increasing their food miles. — "Food miles" luôn ở số nhiều, chỉ quãng đường thực phẩm di chuyển từ nơi sản xuất đến người tiêu dùng — thước đo tác động môi trường. 7. Ancient moralists tended to view overeating as a sign of gluttony rather than as a predictable response to food engineered to be irresistible. — "Gluttony" là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ sự ăn uống vô độ; tính từ tương ứng là "gluttonous", danh từ chỉ người là "glutton". 8. Nutritionists argue that many packaged snacks are specifically designed to delay the feeling of satiety, encouraging people to keep eating long after they are full. — "Satiety" là cảm giác no/thoả mãn sau khi ăn; hay đi với "a feeling of satiety", "reach satiety"; đối lập với "hunger/appetite". 9. Chronic malnutrition is not limited to poorer countries; it can also affect people in wealthier nations who eat plenty of calories but few genuine nutrients. — "Malnutrition" bao gồm cả thiếu và thừa dinh dưỡng mất cân bằng, không chỉ nghĩa "thiếu ăn"; collocation "chronic malnutrition", "suffer from malnutrition". 10. Reading the label on a packet of crisps, I was startled by how many artificial additives were needed simply to keep the flavour consistent. — "Additives" (số nhiều) là các chất được thêm vào thực phẩm để cải thiện hương vị, hình thức hoặc hạn sử dụng; collocation "artificial/food additives". 11. Public health researchers increasingly agree that diets high in salt, sugar and refined carbohydrates can be seriously detrimental to long-term health. — "Detrimental" luôn đi với giới từ "to" (detrimental to health), nghĩa là có hại, gây tổn hại dần dần. 12. Travelling through Vietnam, I was struck by how much regional cuisine varies from north to south, shaped by climate, history and available ingredients. — "Cuisine" là danh từ không đếm được chỉ phong cách/nền ẩm thực đặc trưng của một vùng hay quốc gia; collocation "local/indigenous/fusion cuisine".

PHẦN B: 1. Band 7: Fast food tends to be high in saturated fat and refined sugar, both of which are widely linked to long-term health problems. Band 8: Given its typically high fat and sugar content, it is hardly surprising that fast food is regarded by many nutritionists as detrimental to public health. 2. Band 7: Many people have stopped cooking at home simply because their busy work schedules leave them with very little time to spare. Band 8: So demanding have modern working schedules become that home cooking has, for many time-poor households, been all but replaced by convenience food. 3. Band 7: I would tentatively suggest that people should prioritise locally grown food over imported produce wherever possible. Band 8: Were consumers to prioritise locally sourced produce over imported alternatives, the resulting reduction in food miles would likely bring meaningful environmental benefits. 4. Band 7: Some children consume excessive amounts of sugar partly because advertising tends to present sweet products as fun and desirable. Band 8: It is largely the persuasive architecture of advertising, rather than taste alone, that appears to drive excessive sugar consumption among children. 5. Band 7: Traditional cooking methods seem to be gradually disappearing as younger generations increasingly opt for convenient, ready-made meals. Band 8: What is often mistaken for a simple shift in taste is, in reality, the gradual erosion of traditional culinary heritage under the pressure of convenience culture. 6. Band 7: Governments should arguably introduce stricter regulations to prevent companies from marketing unhealthy food directly to children. Band 8: There is growing concern that, absent stricter regulation, companies will continue to target children with the marketing of nutritionally poor products. 7. Band 7: Emerging agricultural technology could potentially help farmers produce food in ways that place less strain on the environment. Band 8: While technology may well ease the environmental burden of food production, it would be unwise to treat it as a sufficient solution in itself. 8. Band 7: Dining out on a regular basis can prove costly and does not necessarily guarantee a balanced, healthy diet. The Rise of Plant-Based Diets: Concerns over animal cruelty and greenhouse gas emissions from the meat industry have caused a surge in veganism and the development of lab-grown meat alternatives.

The "Sugar Tax": Several countries (like the UK and Mexico) have implemented a levy on sugary drinks, effectively forcing beverage companies to reformulate their recipes and reducing sugar intake nationwide.
Food Waste Epidemic: Approximately one-third of all food produced globally for human consumption is lost or wasted every year, while millions simultaneously suffer from famine.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Local Food vs. Imported Food (Food Miles)

Arguments for Local Food: Significantly reduces "food miles" and greenhouse gas emissions; supports the domestic agricultural economy; fresh produce is more nutritious as it isn't sprayed with heavy preservatives for long transport.
Arguments for Imported Food: Ensures food security and a varied diet year-round, regardless of local seasonal changes; allows developing nations to build their economies through agricultural exports.
Topic: Taxing Unhealthy Foods (Should governments intervene in our diets?)

Arguments FOR (Intervention): The obesity epidemic places a massive financial burden on public healthcare systems; a sugar tax acts as a financial deterrent; the government has a moral duty to protect citizens from predatory fast-food marketing.

Arguments AGAINST (Free Choice): It is a "regressive tax" that disproportionately penalises low-income families who rely on cheap, high-calorie foods; what we eat is a fundamental personal choice, and the state should not act as a "nanny".
Topic: Traditional Meals vs. Fast Food
Traditional Meals: Eating together is a vital social ritual that strengthens family bonds; involves fresh ingredients and passes down culinary heritage.
Fast Food: Caters to the modern, fast-paced lifestyle of dual-income families who lack the time and energy to cook; highly convenient and economical, despite the long-term health risks.

Model answer (≈ 275 words)

The meal that perhaps taught me more about culture than any single experience I can recall was a kaiseki dinner I shared in a small Kyoto ryokan in the autumn of 2023. I was hosted by an old family friend, and what I'd assumed would simply be an elegant evening turned into something approaching a philosophical lesson disguised as cuisine.

Kaiseki, for those unfamiliar, is a multi-course tasting menu rooted in tea-ceremony aesthetics, and what struck me almost immediately was the sheer choreography of it all. Each plate arrived with a seasonal motif — a single maple leaf draped across the sashimi, persimmon-glazed fish hinting at the harvest. The portions were modest, almost austere, yet every element seemed to carry intent. Our host walked us through the principle of mottainai — the cultural injunction against waste — and explained that nothing on the menu was incidental: the bones became broth, the trimmings became garnish.

What I took away wasn't really about food in the narrow sense. It was a quiet but forceful demonstration that gastronomy can function as a vehicle for metaphysical ideas — impermanence, reverence, restraint. The juxtaposition with the commodified, hyper-palatable fare that dominates my own food landscape was, frankly, unsettling. According to the FAO's 2022 figures, roughly a third of all food produced globally is wasted, and standing at that ryokan table, that statistic suddenly felt less like an abstraction and more like a moral failure.

Were I to summarise the meaning of that meal, I'd put it like this: it taught me that culture is most powerfully transmitted not through monuments or museums, but through the small, repeated rituals that surround something as ordinary as dinner.
Examiner follow-up questions
Have you tried to replicate any aspect of that meal at home?
Do you think this kind of dining experience is sustainable globally?
How does this contrast with how meals work in your culture?

Q1. Why are people eating less traditional food?
PEEL answer
Point: The decline is driven not so much by changing tastes as by a structural shift in how labour, time and food retail interact.

Evidence: A 2023 Monteiro et al. study in Nature Food found that ultra-processed food now accounts for over 57% of caloric intake in the US and 30% in middle-income countries — up from roughly 10% three decades ago. The FAO's 2023 SOFI report also documented that dual-income households spend, on average, 40% less time on home cooking than they did in 1990.
Explanation: What this implies is that the erosion of traditional food culture is fundamentally a time-poverty problem, compounded by aggressive marketing of convenience foods.
Link: Reviving traditional foodways therefore requires more than nostalgia — it demands structural intervention.

The FAO's 2023 SOFI report noted that dual-income households spend around 40% less time cooking than in 1990. What this implies is that the erosion of traditional foodways is fundamentally a time-poverty problem — compounded, of course, by aggressive marketing of convenience.
Q2. Should fast food advertising be banned, particularly to children?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd argue a targeted ban on advertising to under-16s is both ethically defensible and empirically supported.

Evidence: Chile's 2016 Food Labelling and Advertising Law, evaluated by Taillie et al. in PLOS Medicine (2020), produced a 24% drop in children's sugary-drink purchases within 18 months. The WHO's 2023 report on marketing of food to children further flagged that exposure to junk-food advertising remains a primary driver of childhood obesity globally.

Explanation: Children, as the marketing-ethics literature consistently shows, lack the cognitive defences against persuasive intent — which makes the libertarian "free speech" defence considerably weaker here.
Link: So while blanket bans may overreach, child-specific restrictions strike me as both proportionate and overdue.
Hedging Toolbox

"The ethical case strikes me as fairly clear..."
"I'd resist a blanket position, but..."

Q3. Can technology solve food sustainability challenges?
PEEL answer
Point: Technology can shift the curve, but I'd be wary of framing it as a standalone solution.

Evidence: A 2023 Nature Food analysis by Tilman et al. estimated that precision agriculture and alternative proteins could, in principle, slash agricultural emissions by 40% by 2050; meanwhile, the FAO's 2022 livestock report still attributes 14.5% of global anthropogenic emissions to livestock alone, and the IPCC AR6 (2023) warned that without dietary shifts, technological gains will largely be cancelled out by rising demand.
Explanation: What this points to is the so-called "Jevons paradox" — efficiency gains tend to be eaten by expanding consumption unless paired with behavioural and policy levers.
Link: Technology is necessary, then, but emphatically not sufficient.

T25 — FOOD & DIET
Lecture title: "From Gluttony to Satiety: Why Ultra-Processed Foods Hijack the Modern Appetite"
1. Section Type
IELTS Listening — Section 4 (single-speaker academic lecture in nutritional science, ~3:00 minutes). Speaker: Dr Idris Okafor, Institute of Food Policy. Note-completion + summary-completion hybrid.
2. Pre-Listening Vocabulary (4–5 words)
3. Predict 3 Ideas
The talk will likely reframe overeating as engineered, not a moral failure.
Ultra-processed foods are designed to bypass the body's natural fullness signals.
Solutions may include sugar taxes or whole-food policy.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Right, settle in — today we're examining how the modern food environment manufactures overconsumption. For most of human history, gluttony was understood as a moral failing. I'd like to persuade you, with evidence, that it's now better understood as an engineered outcome.

> Consider the satiety mechanism. Your gut releases hormones — leptin, peptide YY — that signal fullness to the hypothalamus. Whole foods like an apple or a bowl of oats trigger this cascade efficiently. Ultra-processed products, however — the engineered snacks lining our supermarket aisles — are formulated with what food scientists call hyper-palatability: a precise ratio of refined sugar, industrial fats and sodium that overrides the satiety signal almost entirely.

> The consequence? A landmark NIH trial in 2019 found that subjects on an ultra-processed diet consumed roughly five hundred extra calories per day — without reporting greater hunger or pleasure. Read that again. The food made them eat more without making them happier. That's not weakness; that's neurochemistry being hijacked.

> Now, the policy implications. Several nations — Mexico, the UK, Chile — have implemented a levy on sugary beverages, and the early evidence is genuinely encouraging: a measurable reduction in purchase volume and, crucially, reformulation by manufacturers. Critics call this regressive taxation because it disproportionately affects low-income households. Fair point — though I'd counter that the obesity epidemic is itself profoundly regressive in its health outcomes.

Now, before we get to food miles, I want to dwell on a mechanism that deepens the engineered-overconsumption story in a way that, frankly, I find more disturbing than the satiety hijack alone. It concerns the brain's reward circuitry rather than the gut's. Researchers studying the dopaminergic system have shown that ultra-processed foods deliver what's sometimes called supernormal stimulation — a reward signal more intense than anything our ancestors encountered in nature, because no wild food pairs concentrated fat and rapidly absorbed sugar the way a doughnut does. [pause] Over repeated exposure, the striatum down-regulates its dopamine receptors, much as it does in substance dependence. So the appetite isn't just unsatisfied; it's recalibrated upward. You need more next time to feel the same.

Let me bring in a striking natural experiment, because the sceptic in the room may suspect this is all rodent neuroscience with shaky human relevance. Consider the dietary transition in Indigenous Pima communities, or the shift across Pacific island nations as imported processed staples displaced traditional diets within a single generation. The genetics didn't change in twenty years; the food environment did — and rates of metabolic disease climbed in near-lockstep. Well, that's about as close to a controlled demonstration as epidemiology ever offers us.

There's a counter-position I should honour, though. Industry representatives argue that hyper-palatability is simply consumer preference revealed — that people demonstrably want these products, and that paternalism has no business overriding free choice. Um, and there's a kernel of truth there. But it rather assumes the preference was formed on a level playing field, when the entire premise of today's lecture is that the field has been deliberately tilted — engineered, optimised, A-B-tested against your own neurochemistry. [pause] So the question that ought to detain any serious policymaker is not whether to respect choice, but how to restore the conditions under which choice can be meaningfully free — and that is exactly where the regulatory levers come in…

> The deeper lesson is this: dietary choice is not a free choice when the food environment has been deliberately optimised against you. Nutritional literacy, alongside structural reform, must therefore become a public-health priority. Turn to your handouts, page seven, while I unpack the food-miles dimension…
5. Vocabulary Highlighted (band 8+ topic-specific)

gluttony, satiety, ultra-processed, hyper-palatability, manufactured overconsumption, engineered outcome, leptin, hypothalamus, overrides, hijacked, levy, reformulation, regressive taxation, obesity epidemic, nutritional literacy, food miles, whole foods, refined sugar.
6. Five Questions (≥3 paraphrase)
Q1. (Summary completion — paraphrase)

(Answer: engineered)
Q2. (MCQ — paraphrase)

A. felt much hungrier
B. ate around 500 extra daily calories without enjoying them more
C. gained no weight

Q3. (Short answer — paraphrase)

(Answer: hyper-palatability)
Q4. (MCQ — paraphrase / opinion identification)

A. they are entirely correct and the tax should end
B. obesity itself produces unequal health outcomes
C. low-income families don't drink soda
D. taxation is irrelevant
(Answer: B)
Q5. (Note completion — verbatim-light)

(Answer: nutritional)
7. Listen-For Cues
Q1 cue: the rhetorical pivot "I'd like to persuade you, with evidence…" — signals the lecturer's reframing.
Q2 cue: "Read that again" — emphatic repetition flagging an important statistic.
Q3 cue: definitional phrase "what food scientists call…" — introduces a technical term.
Q4 cue: the concessive "Fair point — though I'd counter…" — signals the speaker's actual stance.
Q5 cue: the deductive marker "The deeper lesson is this:" — flags a thesis statement.

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~198 từ)
The diagram outlines the eight-stage process by which coffee is produced, beginning with cultivation on tropical highland farms and culminating in a brewed cup served to the consumer.

Overall, the process is essentially linear and one-directional, and it can be divided into three broad phases: agricultural production at origin, industrial processing, and final refinement in the consumer country. The early, farm-based stages are notably more labour-intensive than the mechanised stages that follow.

Initially, coffee shrubs are cultivated on highland farms, after which the ripe red cherries are harvested either by hand or by machine. The cherries are then pulped to remove the outer skin and subsequently fermented in water tanks for up to 48 hours in order to dissolve the mucilage. Once fermentation is complete, the beans are sun-dried on patios or in mechanical dryers until their moisture content falls to roughly 11%.

In the next phase, the parchment layer is hulled off and the green beans are graded by size and density before being exported abroad in jute sacks. Finally, in the destination country, the beans are roasted at high temperatures, then ground, packaged and brewed, generating considerable food miles before the coffee reaches the consumer's cup.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~196 từ)
The diagram delineates the eight discrete stages through which coffee is produced, commencing with cultivation on tropical highland farms and culminating in a brewed beverage served to the consumer.

Overall, what is most striking is the uneven distribution of labour across an otherwise linear sequence: the agricultural stages at origin are considerably more labour-intensive than the mechanised processing that follows, so that the journey can be read as three successive phases — farm, factory and café.

Initially, coffee shrubs are cultivated on highland farms, after which the ripe cherries are harvested manually or mechanically. They are subsequently pulped to strip the outer skin and then fermented in water tanks for up to 48 hours, a step that dissolves the residual mucilage. Not until the beans have been sun-dried to a moisture content of around 11% does the produce leave the farm.

Thereafter, the parchment is hulled away and the green beans are graded by size and density before being shipped overseas in jute sacks. Only in the consumer country are they roasted at 200–240°C, after which they are ground, packaged and finally brewed — a chain that accumulates substantial food miles before the cup is served.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 viết Overview ở tầng khái quát cao hơn — không chỉ nói 'linear, ba giai đoạn' mà nhận định về 'phân bố lao động không đều' giữa khâu nông nghiệp và khâu cơ giới hoá, thể hiện Task Achievement vượt trội so với Band 7.

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp dày hơn: đảo ngữ ('Not until the beans have been sun-dried ... does the produce leave the farm', 'Only in the consumer country are they roasted') và lexis chính xác hơn ('delineates', 'discrete stages', 'residual mucilage', 'globe-spanning chain'), trong khi Band 7 dựa nhiều vào 'after which / subsequently / finally' đơn giản.

•  Cả hai bài đều dùng bị động + sequencer đúng chuẩn quy trình, nhưng Band 8 kiểm soát mạch liên kết mượt hơn ('Thereafter ... Only in ... after which') và khép bài bằng nhận định 'food miles' gắn với tính toàn cầu, nâng Coherence một bậc.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)

•  Đọc sơ đồ 30 giây để xác định đây là quy trình TUYẾN TÍNH MỘT CHIỀU và tìm các điểm phân giai đoạn (nông trại → nhà máy → quán/người dùng) — đây là 'mỏ neo' để viết Overview phân loại thay vì đếm bước.
•  Viết Overview bằng hai ý: (1) quy trình tuyến tính một chiều, (2) chia ba giai đoạn (sản xuất tại nguồn / chế biến / hoàn thiện ở nước tiêu thụ) — TUYỆT ĐỐI không nêu tên hay số liệu từng bước.
•  Mặc định dùng thể bị động vì tác nhân không quan trọng ('are cultivated', 'are pulped', 'are fermented', 'are roasted'); chỉ chuyển sang chủ động khi nhấn vai trò con người (nông dân hái).
•  Đa dạng hoá sequencer theo cụm hai: Initially / after which > then / subsequently > Once ... is complete > Thereafter > finally — tránh lặp 'then ... then ... then'.

•  Khép bài bằng ý 'đích đến / mục đích' (cốc cà phê cho người dùng) kèm nhận xét 'food miles', thay vì chỉ kể động từ cuối; dùng phân từ giảm ('Once dried, ...', 'Having been roasted, ...') để nén bước và nâng band.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~270 words)

The sharp rise of ultra-processed food on supermarket shelves has, in recent decades, become a serious public-health concern. This essay will examine the principal drivers behind this trend before suggesting a set of practical measures.

The causes of the crisis appear to be largely structural rather than purely personal. What food companies exploit, above all, is the aggressive marketing of cheap, energy-dense products engineered for hyper-palatability. Such snacks routinely bypass the body's natural feeling of satiety, encouraging overconsumption. In addition, dual-income households often lack the time to prepare meals from scratch, which makes processed alternatives the default option. The result is a rapid rise in obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, particularly in low-income communities where fresh produce is least affordable and where these cheap staples are most heavily promoted.

In terms of remedies, governments must intervene on several fronts. A sugar levy, similar to those introduced in the UK and Mexico, is believed to have pushed beverage companies to reformulate their recipes and trim sugar content nationwide. Clear front-of-pack labelling, together with restrictions on advertising to children, is likely to curb impulse consumption among the most vulnerable shoppers. Beyond such fiscal tools, schools should embed nutritional literacy in the curriculum so that pupils learn to interpret labels and assess food miles.

It is also important that fresh produce be made more affordable through targeted subsidies, otherwise lower-income families will continue to depend on cheaper processed staples. To conclude, the ultra-processed food crisis is driven not so much by individual weakness as by a commercially engineered environment, so a coordinated mix of fiscal, educational and regulatory measures is essential.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~290 words)

The proliferation of ultra-processed food has emerged as one of the defining public-health challenges of our era, implicated in surging rates of obesity, metabolic disease and premature mortality. The causes are largely commercial-structural, and any credible response must combine fiscal, educational and regulatory levers.

The crisis is driven not so much by individual gluttony as by a tightly engineered food environment. Industry data indicate that ultra-processed products now supply a substantial share of dietary energy in many high-income countries, while penetration in middle-income markets is accelerating. So aggressively are these foods reformulated for hyper-palatability that they routinely override innate satiety signals, fostering overconsumption. Compounding this, time-poor dual-income households turn to convenience formats, and the commodification of food has rendered ultra-processed snacks both cheaper and more accessible than fresh, perishable produce — especially in lower-income neighbourhoods.

A coherent policy response is therefore imperative. Sugar and fat levies, such as those operating in the UK and Mexico, are believed to have driven measurable reformulation and modest reductions in consumption. Equally crucial is mandatory front-of-pack labelling, coupled with restrictions on advertising high-fat, salt and sugar products to children, a measure the World Health Organisation has long advocated. What schools must also undertake is the cultivation of genuine nutritional literacy, equipping pupils to interpret labelling, food miles and ingredient lists rather than absorb marketing claims uncritically.

Only if fresh produce is rendered economically competitive — through targeted subsidies and support for short supply chains — will lower-income households realistically shift away from ultra-processed staples. To conclude, the crisis is not a failure of personal discipline but a predictable outcome of commercial incentives and policy neglect; a coordinated, evidence-based mix of taxation, regulation and education offers the most defensible route toward restoring population dietary health.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 mở bài và thesis ở register cao và sắc hơn ('one of the defining public-health challenges of our era', 'commercial-structural') và neo bằng dữ liệu định lượng ('a substantial share of dietary energy', 'penetration in middle-income markets'), nâng Task Response so với mở bài thủ tục của Band 7.

•  Band 8 dùng dày cấu trúc bậc cao và chính xác: đảo ngữ ('So aggressively are these foods reformulated that ...', 'Only if fresh produce is rendered economically competitive will ...'), câu chẻ ('What schools must also undertake is ...'), cấu trúc 'not so much ... as ...' và danh hoá ('the commodification of food has rendered ...'), trong khi Band 7 chủ yếu dùng một cleft và liên kết phẳng hơn.

•  Band 8 nâng lexis lên bậc chuyên ngành ('metabolic disease', 'premature mortality', 'perishable', 'short supply chains', 'commodification') và cohesion mượt hơn ('Compounding this ... Equally crucial is ... Only if ... will ...'), trong khi Band 7 giữ một số cụm trung tính hơn ('on several fronts', 'It is also important that'), khiến Band 8 vượt rõ về Lexical Resource lẫn Coherence.

Thực phẩm chính, lương thực cơ bản trong chế độ ăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Rice remains the **staple** diet for more than half of the world's population.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"staple" (cái ghim/vật cơ bản giữ mọi thứ lại) → thực phẩm "cốt lõi" của một chế độ ăn.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi làm tính từ trước danh từ ('staple diet', 'staple food'), không thêm '-s'; danh từ số nhiều là 'staples'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a main or important element of a diet, especially a food eaten regularly as a dietary basis
vocabulary.definition_vi: thực phẩm chính, lương thực cơ bản
vocabulary.example: Rice remains the staple diet for more than half of the world's population.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'staple' (cái ghim/vật cơ bản giữ mọi thứ lại) → thực phẩm 'cốt lõi' của một chế độ ăn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quãng đường vận chuyển thực phẩm, thước đo tác động môi trường của chuỗi cung ứng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Importing exotic fruits from across the globe drastically increases our **food miles**, contributing to carbon emissions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"food" (thực phẩm) + "miles" (dặm đường) → số dặm thực phẩm phải di chuyển để đến tay người tiêu dùng.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng số nhiều 'food miles', không dùng số ít 'food mile' dù chỉ nói về một loại thực phẩm cụ thể.
vocabulary.definition_en: the total distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed, often used as a measure of environmental impact
vocabulary.definition_vi: quãng đường vận chuyển thực phẩm (đo tác động môi trường)
vocabulary.example: Importing exotic fruits from across the globe drastically increases our food miles, contributing to carbon emissions.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'food' (thực phẩm) + 'miles' (dặm đường) → số dặm thực phẩm phải di chuyển để đến tay người tiêu dùng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự háu ăn, ăn uống vô độ, quá mức cần thiết.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Historically, overeating was viewed as a moral failing rooted in **gluttony** rather than an engineered outcome.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Một trong "7 mối tội đầu" theo Kinh Thánh → "gluttony" = ăn uống vô độ, tham lam trong ăn uống.
vocabulary.common_error: Là danh từ trừu tượng không đếm được; tính từ tương ứng là 'gluttonous', danh từ chỉ người là 'glutton'.
vocabulary.definition_en: habitual greed or excess in eating; overconsumption of food and drink
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự háu ăn, ăn uống vô độ
vocabulary.example: Historically, overeating was viewed as a moral failing rooted in gluttony rather than an engineered outcome.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Một trong '7 mối tội đầu' theo Kinh Thánh → 'gluttony' = ăn uống vô độ, tham lam trong ăn uống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cảm giác no, thoả mãn sau khi ăn, báo hiệu cơ thể ngừng tiêu thụ thức ăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Ultra-processed snacks are engineered to bypass our natural feeling of **satiety**, making us eat more than we need.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"satiate" (làm no, thoả mãn) + "-ety" → trạng thái đã được thoả mãn cơn đói.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'satiety' (cảm giác no) với 'society' (xã hội) — dễ nhầm khi nghe do phát âm gần giống.
vocabulary.definition_en: the feeling of being full or satisfied after eating, signalling the body to stop consuming food
vocabulary.definition_vi: cảm giác no, thoả mãn sau khi ăn
vocabulary.example: Ultra-processed snacks are engineered to bypass our natural feeling of satiety, making us eat more than we need.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'satiate' (làm no, thoả mãn) + '-ety' → trạng thái đã được thoả mãn cơn đói.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Suy dinh dưỡng, tình trạng dinh dưỡng không cân bằng hoặc thiếu hụt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Chronic **malnutrition** continues to affect millions of children in regions facing food insecurity.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"mal-" (xấu, sai) + "nutrition" (dinh dưỡng) → tình trạng dinh dưỡng không đúng cách, dù thiếu hay thừa.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Malnutrition' bao gồm cả thiếu VÀ thừa dinh dưỡng mất cân bằng, không chỉ giới hạn ở nghĩa 'thiếu ăn' như nhiều người hiểu.
vocabulary.definition_en: a lack of proper nutrition, caused by insufficient, excessive, or unbalanced diet
vocabulary.definition_vi: suy dinh dưỡng
vocabulary.example: Chronic malnutrition continues to affect millions of children in regions facing food insecurity.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'mal-' (xấu, sai) + 'nutrition' (dinh dưỡng) → tình trạng dinh dưỡng không đúng cách, dù thiếu hay thừa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phụ gia thực phẩm, chất được thêm vào để cải thiện hoặc bảo quản.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Artificial **additives** are used to extend the shelf life of many supermarket products.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"add" (thêm vào) + "-itive" → chất được "thêm vào" thực phẩm để cải thiện hoặc bảo quản.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ đếm được, số nhiều 'additives'; tính từ ghép 'additive-free' cần gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: a substance added to food in small amounts to improve or preserve its flavour, appearance, or shelf life
vocabulary.definition_vi: phụ gia (thực phẩm)
vocabulary.example: Artificial additives are used to extend the shelf life of many supermarket products.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'add' (thêm vào) + '-itive' → chất được 'thêm vào' thực phẩm để cải thiện hoặc bảo quản.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Người chỉ ăn thực phẩm được trồng hoặc sản xuất ở địa phương.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **locavore** movement encourages consumers to reduce food miles by buying from nearby farms.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"local" (địa phương) + "-vore" (ăn, như carnivore) → người chỉ ăn thực phẩm được sản xuất gần nơi mình sống.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm hậu tố '-vore' (người/vật ăn gì đó, như trong 'carnivore') với '-vour' trong 'devour' — chính tả khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who tries to eat only food that is grown or produced locally
vocabulary.definition_vi: người ăn thực phẩm địa phương (hạn chế thực phẩm nhập khẩu xa)
vocabulary.example: The locavore movement encourages consumers to reduce food miles by buying from nearby farms.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'local' (địa phương) + '-vore' (ăn, như carnivore) → người chỉ ăn thực phẩm được sản xuất gần nơi mình sống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có hại, gây tổn hại, đặc biệt đến sức khoẻ hoặc sự phát triển.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A diet high in refined sugar and salt can be seriously **detrimental** to long-term health.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin "deterere" (mài mòn) → detrimental = gây hao mòn, tổn hại dần dần.
vocabulary.common_error: Giới từ bắt buộc là 'to' ('detrimental to health'), không dùng 'for' hay 'on'.
vocabulary.definition_en: tending to cause harm or damage, especially to health or well-being
vocabulary.definition_vi: có hại, gây tổn hại (đến sức khoẻ)
vocabulary.example: A diet high in refined sugar and salt can be seriously detrimental to long-term health.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Latin 'deterere' (mài mòn) → detrimental = gây hao mòn, tổn hại dần dần.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nền ẩm thực, phong cách nấu ăn đặc trưng của một vùng hoặc quốc gia.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Indigenous **cuisine** often reflects centuries of adaptation to local ingredients and climate.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Mượn từ tiếng Pháp "cuisine" (nhà bếp, nấu ăn) → phong cách ẩm thực đặc trưng của một vùng.
vocabulary.common_error: Phát âm là /kwɪˈziːn/ (gốc Pháp), không phát âm theo quy tắc tiếng Anh thông thường; là danh từ không đếm được.
vocabulary.definition_en: a style or method of cooking, especially as characteristic of a particular country or region
vocabulary.definition_vi: nền ẩm thực (đặc trưng của một vùng/quốc gia)
vocabulary.example: Indigenous cuisine often reflects centuries of adaptation to local ingredients and climate.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Mượn từ tiếng Pháp 'cuisine' (nhà bếp, nấu ăn) → phong cách ẩm thực đặc trưng của một vùng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Siêu chế biến, thực phẩm công nghiệp với nhiều phụ gia và ít thành phần tự nhiên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Participants eating **ultra-processed** food in the 2019 NIH trial ate around 500 extra daily calories without enjoying them more.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"ultra-" (cực kỳ) + "processed" (đã qua chế biến) → thực phẩm trải qua chế biến công nghiệp ở mức cao nhất.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn có gạch nối 'ultra-processed' khi đứng trước danh từ; phân biệt với 'processed' đơn thuần (chế biến ở mức độ nhẹ hơn).
vocabulary.definition_en: (of food) industrially manufactured using multiple ingredients and additives, with minimal whole-food content
vocabulary.definition_vi: siêu chế biến (thực phẩm công nghiệp, nhiều phụ gia)
vocabulary.example: Participants eating ultra-processed food in the 2019 NIH trial ate around 500 extra daily calories without enjoying them more.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'ultra-' (cực kỳ) + 'processed' (đã qua chế biến) → thực phẩm trải qua chế biến công nghiệp ở mức cao nhất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tính siêu hấp dẫn vị giác, được thiết kế để vượt qua tín hiệu no tự nhiên của cơ thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The engineered ratio of sugar, fat and salt known as **hyper-palatability** defeats the body's natural fullness response.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"hyper-" (cực độ) + "palatability" (độ ngon miệng) → độ ngon miệng được đẩy lên mức cực đoan, khiến ta ăn quá đà.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn có gạch nối 'hyper-palatability'; đừng nhầm với 'palpability' (tính có thể sờ/cảm nhận được) — hai từ khác nghĩa hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.definition_en: an engineered combination of sugar, fat and salt designed to be intensely pleasurable and to override natural satiety signals
vocabulary.definition_vi: tính siêu hấp dẫn vị giác (được thiết kế để vượt qua cảm giác no)
vocabulary.example: The engineered ratio of sugar, fat and salt known as hyper-palatability defeats the body's natural fullness response.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'hyper-' (cực độ) + 'palatability' (độ ngon miệng) → độ ngon miệng được đẩy lên mức cực đoan, khiến ta ăn quá đà.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vấn đề cấp bách, cần được quan tâm và giải quyết ngay.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The rise of ultra-processed diets has become **a pressing concern** for public health authorities worldwide.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"press" (thúc ép, tạo áp lực) + "concern" (mối lo) → mối lo đang tạo áp lực buộc phải giải quyết ngay.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Pressing' ở đây là tính từ (cấp bách), không nhầm với động từ 'press' (ép, nhấn) trong nghĩa đen.
vocabulary.definition_en: an issue that urgently needs attention or action
vocabulary.definition_vi: vấn đề cấp bách cần được quan tâm
vocabulary.example: The rise of ultra-processed diets has become a pressing concern for public health authorities worldwide.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'press' (thúc ép, tạo áp lực) + 'concern' (mối lo) → mối lo đang tạo áp lực buộc phải giải quyết ngay.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Điều đáng suy ngẫm, khiến người ta phải nghiêm túc suy nghĩ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The documentary about the meat industry gave me plenty of **food for thought** regarding my own eating habits.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"food" (thức ăn) nuôi cơ thể, còn "food for thought" là "thức ăn" nuôi dưỡng tâm trí, khiến ta suy nghĩ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Thought' trong cụm này không đếm được, không thêm 's'; luôn dùng với động từ 'give/provide'.
vocabulary.definition_en: something that makes you think seriously about a subject
vocabulary.definition_vi: điều đáng suy ngẫm
vocabulary.example: The documentary about the meat industry gave me plenty of food for thought regarding my own eating habits.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'food' (thức ăn) nuôi cơ thể, còn 'food for thought' là 'thức ăn' nuôi dưỡng tâm trí, khiến ta suy nghĩ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thích ăn đồ ngọt, nghiện vị ngọt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I **have a massive sweet tooth**, so I can never say no to chocolate cake.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"sweet" (ngọt) + "tooth" (răng) → như thể có một "chiếc răng" luôn thèm vị ngọt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Tooth' trong thành ngữ này luôn ở số ít, dù nói về nhiều loại đồ ngọt; không đổi thành 'teeth'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to have a strong preference or craving for sweet foods
vocabulary.definition_vi: thích ăn đồ ngọt, nghiện đồ ngọt
vocabulary.example: I have a massive sweet tooth, so I can never say no to chocolate cake.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sweet' (ngọt) + 'tooth' (răng) → như thể có một 'chiếc răng' luôn thèm vị ngọt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nên hoài nghi, không nên tin hoàn toàn vào điều gì đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> You should take his nutrition advice **with a pinch of salt**; he is not a qualified doctor.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Một "nhúm muối" ("pinch of salt") làm nhạt bớt vị của câu chuyện → nghe nhưng đừng tin hoàn toàn.
collocations: take sth with a pinch of salt
take a claim with a grain of salt (US variant)
vocabulary.common_error: Biến thể Anh-Mỹ dùng 'a grain of salt' thay vì 'a pinch of salt'; trong Anh-Anh chuẩn dùng 'pinch'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to not fully believe something, regarding it with a degree of scepticism
vocabulary.definition_vi: nên hoài nghi, không nên tin hoàn toàn
vocabulary.example: You should take his nutrition advice with a pinch of salt; he is not a qualified doctor.
vocabulary.headword: Take with a pinch of salt
vocabulary.memory_hook: Một 'nhúm muối' ('pinch of salt') làm nhạt bớt vị của câu chuyện → nghe nhưng đừng tin hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.syllables: take with a PINCH of SALT

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ôm đồm quá sức, nhận công việc vượt quá khả năng xử lý.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I think I **bit off more than I could chew** by accepting three heavy projects at once.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Cắn ("bite") một miếng quá to để có thể nhai ("chew") hết → nhận việc quá sức mình có thể xử lý.
collocations: bite off more than one can chew
vocabulary.common_error: Thì quá khứ là 'bit off... could chew', không phải 'bited'; động từ bất quy tắc 'bite → bit → bitten'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to take on a task or commitment that is too large or difficult to manage
vocabulary.definition_vi: ôm đồm quá sức, nhận việc vượt quá khả năng
vocabulary.example: I think I bit off more than I could chew by accepting three heavy projects at once.
vocabulary.headword: Bite off more than one can chew
vocabulary.memory_hook: Cắn ('bite') một miếng quá to để có thể nhai ('chew') hết → nhận việc quá sức mình có thể xử lý.
vocabulary.pronunciation: /baɪt ɒf mɔː ðən wʌn kən tʃuː/
vocabulary.syllables: bite off more than one can CHEW

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chuyện dễ như ăn bánh, việc rất đơn giản để hoàn thành.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Don't worry about the cooking exam tomorrow; it will be **a piece of cake**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ăn một "miếng bánh" ("piece of cake") rất dễ và ngon → việc gì đó dễ dàng, không tốn sức.
collocations: find sth a piece of cake
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn có mạo từ 'a' trước cụm 'a piece of cake'; không dùng số nhiều 'pieces of cake' trong nghĩa thành ngữ.
vocabulary.definition_en: something very easy to do or accomplish
vocabulary.definition_vi: chuyện dễ như ăn bánh, việc rất đơn giản
vocabulary.example: Don't worry about the cooking exam tomorrow; it will be a piece of cake.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Ăn một 'miếng bánh' ('piece of cake') rất dễ và ngon → việc gì đó dễ dàng, không tốn sức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiết lộ bí mật, thường là vô tình hoặc quá sớm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We are throwing a surprise party for him, so please don't **spill the beans**!

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Làm đổ ("spill") những hạt đậu ("beans") ra khỏi túi → để lộ bí mật ra ngoài một cách vô tình.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Beans' luôn ở số nhiều trong thành ngữ này; không dùng số ít 'spill the bean'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to reveal secret information, often unintentionally or prematurely
vocabulary.definition_vi: tiết lộ bí mật (thường là vô tình)
vocabulary.example: We are throwing a surprise party for him, so please don't spill the beans!
vocabulary.memory_hook: Làm đổ ('spill') những hạt đậu ('beans') ra khỏi túi → để lộ bí mật ra ngoài một cách vô tình.
synonyms: let the cat out of the bag

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ăn rất khoẻ, ăn với lượng thức ăn lớn thường xuyên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He is very thin, but he has a huge appetite and **eats like a horse**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ngựa ("horse") là loài ăn rất nhiều cỏ mỗi ngày → "eat like a horse" = ăn với sức chứa lớn.
collocations: he eats like a horse but never gains weight
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ so sánh cố định với 'horse'; đối lập trực tiếp là 'eat like a bird' (ăn rất ít), không phải phủ định đơn thuần.
vocabulary.definition_en: to eat a very large amount of food regularly
vocabulary.definition_vi: ăn rất khoẻ, ăn như tằm ăn rỗi
vocabulary.example: He is very thin, but he has a huge appetite and eats like a horse.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Ngựa ('horse') là loài ăn rất nhiều cỏ mỗi ngày → 'eat like a horse' = ăn với sức chứa lớn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Không hợp gu, không phải sở thích của một người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I know many people love spicy food, but it's simply **not my cup of tea**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Trà ("tea") là thức uống mang tính cá nhân, mỗi người một gu → điều gì "not one's cup of tea" là không hợp khẩu vị riêng của họ.
collocations: definitely not my cup of tea
vocabulary.common_error: Sở hữu cách phải khớp chủ ngữ: 'not MY cup of tea', 'not HIS cup of tea', không dùng mạo từ 'the' thay vào.
vocabulary.definition_en: used to say that something is not to one's taste or liking
vocabulary.definition_vi: không hợp gu, không phải sở thích của ai đó
vocabulary.example: I know many people love spicy food, but it's simply not my cup of tea.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Trà ('tea') là thức uống mang tính cá nhân, mỗi người một gu → điều gì 'not one's cup of tea' là không hợp khẩu vị riêng của họ.
